title: Humanity and Divine Capacity
english: He contemplates and scientifically applies what knowledge is, and what the 'mystery of the kingdom' is, which this one sings. Again, as many as practice—and this alone is what they stand at until they practice—they sing; as we said also concerning the rams, that they have a life that is well-proportioned, but if they are not led, they have neither a life nor the necessary works of life. He sings.

But he who both sings and practices, and sings and contemplates: if he begins from practicing, it is a psalm of song; but if from contemplating, it is a song of a psalm. We see these things happening: often some, wishing to contemplate, stand at the virtues and their works, and taking from the standing itself the possibility to succeed, they come to the practicing. It has become a song of a psalm. The song led, the contemplation.

'Having desired wisdom, he kept the commandments' (Ps 119:2); the one desiring saw; he kept the commandments, he sang; and again he has songs being provided to him. It happens therefore sometimes to begin from the song and receive the psalm, and again he, the psalm having made a way for the soul, again brings a song. If therefore the beginning and the thought of the beginning arise from work as a craft, it is a psalm of song; but when someone, having begun from contemplation, receives the desire to live according to virtue, it is a song of a psalm.

It was necessary therefore for the one being brought in to inaugurate the house to dance thus for the inauguration of the house. This is called a sequence. And sequence is when the one follows the other and does not turn back. But if the following turns back, as it happens that the former becomes the follower and the latter becomes the leader, it is a sequence. The 'to David' indeed refers to this one who succeeded, to whom the victory and the hymn are referred, or to the singer himself. Even if the singer says it, it seems he speaks from the Holy Spirit.

It is not the same to say that 'a man says' and 'a learned man says'; for when we say a man is the one announcing, the things announced are human, but when [we say] a learned man, they are knowledgeable. The knowledge is subordinate to him, and he becomes as a servant of the knowledge. The 'worthy' one therefore 'with hand' sings this psalm or this song, the psalm of the song or again. And every practical man is 'worthy' 'by hand'. But the Savior most especially has this; and g...

But others receive capacity from him. John, indeed, looking at his greatness, said: 'I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals.' Again, if capacity is given from him: 'Our capacity is from God, who made us worthy to be ministers of a new covenant.' Those who are driven to this and seized by love of the matter become imitators of Christ, seeing him acting 'competently' and they themselves act 'competently' according to what is possible for them.

He began saying in the Psalms that what is said about the man whom the Savior took up, might be said about every imitator of him, not only what is said about him as the only-begotten Son and the Word of God; it might be said—I do not speak about humans, nor even about rulers, but about no created thing at all. What is now being said fits the man of the Savior; therefore also others are able to do these things. 'I will exalt you, Lord, because you have lifted me up' (Psalm 30:1). What I have said many times, and now I say: what is said about God, is understood as being about God; but what is said about humans, is understood as being about humans.

Sometimes, what is said about humans, if not as mortals and as men, but as rational beings, is said, and about angels and generally about every spiritual substance; for according to the spiritual, man is of the same kind, according to the capacity for becoming perfect, 'just as the Father in the heavens is perfect' (Matt 5:48). For what more can an angel bear fruit according to what is possible? Then the Savior says to men that I and my Father will come, 'and we will make a single dwelling with him.' What more has a diligent angel to acquire? And furthermore: 'Give, that just as I and you are one, these may be one in us' (John 17:21). What more has the higher being to acquire? We take the difference according to more bodily things: the angel does not have flesh. But it is not the meaning of being rational for man to have flesh, since all things having flesh are rational.

See then: if, therefore, it says among us about being exalted from a lowly place to a higher one and being moved upward above, it is necessary first to change the place. It is impossible for one not changing place to be exalted or to be humbled, I speak locally. When therefore the saint says: 'I will exalt you', this he says: I will give thanks to you. If anyone thinks of Christ according to...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Healing Ointment and Immediate Response
english: Not according to the flesh, but when one no longer perceives according to the flesh, but beholds 'his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (cf. John 1:14), and knows that he who has seen the Son sees the Father, and this is to exalt him.

Therefore, because he says this graciously, the following is brought forward: 'because you have taken me up' (John 14:19); having taken me up, you exalted me. When I was exalted, then I knew your height.

And this can also be seen from things held in the hands; one approaches by skill; not yet the magnitude, not yet the beauty, not yet the height of it he sees. But if he begins to grasp it and is improved by taking in each part with what has already been made known, then seeing the magnitude and the height of the skill and the art, he exalts it, that is, he confesses its height.

For indeed, when he stands over the height and magnitude, he sees much remaining to himself. 'Your knowledge was marveled at from me; it was strengthened, I am not able toward it' (Eccl. 6:18). As much as I stand over it and marvel at it, it becomes strong, and I am no longer able toward it, as long as I am in a body.

This also Solomon says concerning wisdom: 'I said, I will be wise, and it was lengthened far beyond what it was, and a deep depth, who will find it?' (Eccl. 6:18). It was far from me, and when I desired to receive it, it became far from me beyond what it was before. And therefore he gives the reason: 'a deep depth, who will find it?' The 'who will find' may mean 'no one.' And the 'who' is the smallness and not a joy to my enemies upon me. Many enemies lie in wait for me, intending to harm me.

And they were saying that these things are also commonly said concerning the man the Savior and of those imitating him. And the saints had enemies and the Savior had enemies. And no one at all is able to approach him according to the divinity, in order that he might be tested to harm him. And to hate is to approach not for the sake of another but to harm.

And therefore, in the person of Jesus, it is said according to the man and of every imitator and of his member becoming [so]: 'because you have taken me up' (John 14:19); for if you had not taken me up, my enemies would have rejoiced having taken me in hand, and would not have exalted you. It is also possible from the person of the Savior, no longer dividing us and saying according to God the Word or according to man, as we were fully saying concerning the skilled man: 'I will exalt...'

You, Lord, have taken me; you took those two for me, for whom I cried out (Ps 132:13). 'Behold, I and the children, which God has given to me' and 'I will give you the nations for your inheritance' (Ps 2:8). The Savior regards this as his own contest and his own benefit; therefore 'I have not rejoiced my enemies' (Ps 69:20). For the captives were snatched away because of me, and on my account, and on account of those holding them, I will exalt you, but they do not rejoice.

Lord my God, I cried to you, and heal me (Ps 130:1-2). The voice has been heard; for if he cried concerning healing, he already received what he desired. 'I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you' (Ps 130:1-2). He had not yet been healed, for he who says this is confessing and repenting. The face of the Savior says this: 'I cried to you, and heal me'; I received an ointment, therapeutic and medicinal 'for every disease and weakness.' Why then did I have the ointment? So that he himself might become a medicine for those who were wounded. Then my healing occurs when the ointment heals others being my body. 'Lord' therefore 'my God, I cried to you, and heal me.' If each of the righteous says this, he will be heard by him to whom he cries. 'While you are still speaking, I will say, Behold, I am here.' The 'I will say, Behold, I am here' shows the work for which you are worthy, I find myself present to you; for your prayer does not delay my gift, but it happens at once; you have prayed, you have the thing. Let us take examples from the Scriptures; a leper came to the Savior saying, 'If you wish, you are able to cleanse me' (Lk 5:17). He says, 'I will, be cleansed'; and the cleansing happened as if there were no delay. By thought alone previously the worthiness occurred before the cleansing, not by time before. Again: 'Do you wish to be well?' Immediately: 'Rise, take up your bed and walk' (Lk 5:17). And the work of Jesus's command did not happen a second later. You know that the reflection imitates the thing seen, and it is not possible to say which is first, but by thought.

Lord, you brought up my soul from Hades (Ps 138:3). Having healed me, you brought up my soul from Hades. This could be said concerning Jesus; since I had an ointment and was wounded because of certain sins—perhaps those having sins in Hades—they descended there, so that the ointment, having approached...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Confession and the Life in His Will
english: May he heal them. For the healing is the bringing up of my soul from there. I became there not to remain myself, but neither to simply depart and return, but to lead up those there. 'Having been put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit, in which he also preached the message to the spirits in prison' (1 Peter 3:19), he led them up. And because of these things he went down there, and because of these things he says he is ascending; for he went down to lead up. If he were not ascending them, he would not have gone up there; for he did not descend or ascend for his own sake.

And this can also be said: the soul is truly our rational being. As it is said of a certain man of God, so it might be said of a soul. 'You have brought up my soul from Hades' (Psalm 42:5). You saved me from those descending into the pit (Psalm 49:15). Those descending into the pit are called the days, because those above are fallen; for the pits are not springs; they do not have water being supplied from anywhere. And Hades because of this is continually called a pit in the Scriptures, because the souls that fall there are falling.

'You saved me from those descending into the pit' (Psalm 49:15). For even if I descended into Hades, I was not seized in the pit like the falling waters, but I was saved, so that what happens to those falling into Hades does not exceed my harm. 'Praise the Lord, you saints of his' (Psalm 149:5). Therefore, while praising and extolling because he was received, he intends to fall upon the hymn even those whom he led up from Hades, the saints having been shown; for those around Abraham and the other saints were there.

And other souls were there too, but some were shown to be the souls of saints, and others were not; for we do not say that the Savior sanctified all, but those souls which were awaiting him there. They were saying, therefore, toward: 'Are you the one coming, or do we await another?' That man knew he was about to die; for being in the prison, he sent this voice, asking: 'Are you coming there yourself, or are you sending another?' Not that he was doubting, but he wished to serve there beside him, having learned from him, being commanded by him. He writes to the saints: the achievement is for us or is common to us and you. Just as therefore I sing a psalm, you also praise; you join in with instruments to our song, which I send up on behalf of you, saying.

“I will exalt you, O Lord.” 5 And you confess the memory of His holiness. Confession here is not called the disclosure of sins; for this too is called confession, as if one says, “Confess your sins to one another” (Ps 50:4). But most often in Scripture, confession is signified by the word thanksgiving: “We will confess to You, O God, we will confess to You” (Ps 106:1). The memory is moved here by dogmas, he says, “of His holiness.” Discipleship-remembrances are not now but before. If anyone is sanctified, having shared in the holy, he has obtained holiness. And so it has happened, so that one might be holy not by essence, but by choice, having received the holy and the good in advance. Therefore, do not neglect, while confessing and singing, that holiness is your own; because you have become [it], take hold of it; you have become [it] so that you might be holy, not profane; yet you have become in filth and profanity. Reclaim your holiness, and thus desire to become [it].

6 For wrath is in His mind and life is in His will (Ps 30:5). Because of this, I urge you to sing as those having become holy and to confess the memory of His holiness, “for wrath is in His mind” (Ps 30:5), so that you do not fall into wrath and anger; for if you remain in the same [state] as before my arrival, having me having accomplished so much, and in the same [state] regarding the things for which I have come, He will receive wrath, because after so many helps and so many benefits and exhortations you remain in the same [state]. And just as it becomes like wrath in the mind, so also “life is in His will” (Ps 30:5). He who follows His will and works it, asking to know it from Him—indeed, someone sends a prayer saying, “Teach me to do Your will” (Ps 119:35). Through saying with a reason, “For You are my God” (Ps 73:28), it is shown that the will of God is alone life. And our own will must also cooperate, so that He does not say, “How often I willed, and you did not will.” Therefore, “life” is “in Your will.” The Word God can also be said to be will here. In Him all things came to be; all things through Him came into being. In the will, therefore, of Him who brought you into existence, life lies. 6 Weeping shall turn to joy in the evening and in the morning (Ps 30:5).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
